questions.q: What did Green and Brock's research on narrative transportation find?
choices: Absorbed readers held more story-consistent beliefs and spotted fewer false notes
Stories release oxytocin
Fiction readers are always more empathetic
Stories have no persuasive effect
questions.explain: Transportation lowers counterarguing; later meta-analyses found modest but real effects.

questions.q: A seminar promises a 'neuroscience-proven' 15-beat structure. What's the fairest response?
choices: Accept it; brain scans settle craft questions
Reject all research on story
Be skeptical: research supports broad claims, not precise craft prescriptions
Only trust it if it mentions oxytocin
questions.explain: Studies rarely test craft choices directly.

questions.q: What happened to the 2013 study finding that reading literary fiction improves mind-reading?
choices: It became the basis of the Bechdel test
Later replication attempts largely failed
It was proven by brain imaging
It was never published
questions.explain: Correlational evidence about heavy readers is more stable but can't show cause.

questions.q: Why is 'stories work by releasing oxytocin' a weak claim?
choices: Oxytocin doesn't exist in humans
The oxytocin-trust findings haven't replicated well and blood measures are questioned
It was disproven by Aristotle
It applies only to film
questions.explain: A 2015 critical review found the trust evidence wasn't robust.

questions.q: Which statement about storytelling's evolution is most accurate?
choices: It's proven that fiction evolved for social rehearsal
It's proven to be a by-product
Storytelling isn't universal
It's universal, but whether it's an adaptation or a by-product is debated
questions.explain: Boyd and Gottschall argue adaptation; others favor by-product.

questions.q: Why does narrative persuasion research matter especially to journalists?
choices: Because stories always tell the truth
Because absorbed readers argue back less, so a story can carry a weak claim past their guard
Because it shows readers prefer statistics
Because it forbids anecdotal ledes
questions.explain: Story is powerful, which is a responsibility.

questions.q: What did Stephens, Silbert and Hasson's 2010 study report?
choices: Listeners' brain activity coupled with the storyteller's, more so when they understood the story
Stories cause permanent brain change
Literary fiction boosts empathy
Oxytocin doubles during climaxes
questions.explain: Fascinating, but it doesn't yet translate into structural advice.

questions.q: Which is the most balanced verdict on the science of story?
choices: It proves every craft rule
It shows nothing at all
Broad claims hold up; precise mechanisms and craft rules mostly don't yet
It only applies to children

ideas: Which approach measures how absorbed readers are in a story and finds that absorption lowers counterarguing?
Which approach treats fiction as an evolved form of cognitive play that trains attention and social understanding?
Which approach likens stories to a flight simulator for social life?
